name: Reid Hoffman
milestone_by_age_26: Entrepreneurial fame arrived after age 26: co-founded SocialNet in 1997 (age ~30), joined PayPal full-time as COO in 2000 (age ~32), and co-founded LinkedIn in 2002–2003 (age ~35–36). By 26 he had Stanford Symbolic Systems (1990) and a Marshall Scholarship Oxford MSt (1993), but no dated founding/product breakout at or before 26 was identified.

Joined Apple (eWorld) in 1994 at age ~26–27, then Fujitsu, before founding SocialNet (1997) and later PayPal/LinkedIn leadership roles.

parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were attorneys; no clear software/entrepreneurship domain transfer is documented in reviewed sources beyond general professional-class context.
evidence_summary: Strong elite education and eventual PayPal Mafia/LinkedIn success are well documented, but the material company-building milestones fall after age 26. Apple employment beginning ~1994 is borderline on age and is ordinary employment rather than a clear breakout founding milestone.

name: Andrew Barto
milestone_by_age_26: Foundational reinforcement-learning career milestones occurred after age 26: PhD in 1975 (age ~27), UMass postdoc from 1977 (age ~29), and co-development of modern RL with Richard Sutton over subsequent decades (textbook 1998; Turing Award with Sutton for 2024). evidence_summary: Later recognition is extraordinary (Turing Award), but timeline shows PhD and research career launch after 26; undergraduate degree alone is not treated as a material domain breakout for this rubric.

name: Robin Walker
milestone_by_age_26: Co-created the Quake multiplayer mod Team Fortress (released August 1996) with John Cook and Ian Caughley while about age 20–21; the mod's popularity led Valve to hire the team and later ship Team Fortress Classic and Team Fortress 2.
early_history_summary: Walker grew up in rural Australia with early access to a computer rather than TV, and has an older brother who became a programmer. He and childhood friend John Cook began serious game hacking as a hobby; while programming at NEC and mid-way through a computer-science course at RMIT, they built Team Fortress as the multiplayer class-based mod they wanted to play. Player and industry interest by roughly age 21–22 was strong enough to turn the hobby into Team Fortress Software and then a Valve career.
secondary_engine: Complementary peer team / early online mod community
family_context_summary: Grew up in a forested rural area of Australia without a television but with a computer; has an elder brother who worked as a programmer and a younger sister in tertiary education. Detailed parental occupations not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond an older brother who programmed and ran a MUD; parental domain expertise not evidenced.
primary_early_advantage_tags: childhood cofounder John Cook, Quake modding community, early home computer, Team Fortress Software, Valve hire
evidence_summary: Walker and longtime collaborator John Cook (friends since early childhood) built Team Fortress as a Quake mod in 1996 while Walker was about 21, after years of hobby game hacking and concurrent NEC programming work. Contemporary interview sources quote him at age 21 describing rural computer-centric childhood and deferring university when TF interest enabled full-time work. Valve hired the team; Walker became a long-time Valve design lead on Team Fortress Classic, TF2, and later Half-Life: Alyx. Early advantages center on high-trust peer collaboration and immersion in the Quake modding/distribution wave rather than elite institutions or family capital.
starting_point: Raised in rural Australia with early computer access and a programmer older brother; childhood friend and later cofounder John Cook; studied computer science at RMIT before deferring.
current_position: Longtime Valve design manager/designer associated with the Team Fortress series and later Half-Life: Alyx; remains a public Valve design figure as of mid-2020s.

trajectory.event: Co-released Quake Team Fortress, a class-based multiplayer mod that rapidly became one of the era's most popular mods.
Hired by Valve with Team Fortress collaborators after industry interest in the mod's success.
Shipped Team Fortress Classic on Valve's GoldSrc engine, bringing TF to the Half-Life audience.
Released Team Fortress 2 as part of The Orange Box, becoming a flagship multiplayer franchise.
Helped evolve TF2 into a free-to-play, microtransaction-driven live service with ongoing community economy design.
Contributed design leadership on Valve's VR flagship Half-Life: Alyx.

name: Donald Bitzer
category: Electrical engineer / computer scientist / PLATO pioneer
milestone_by_age_26: Led development of PLATO I (Programmed Logic for Automatic Teaching Operations), the pioneering computer-based education system that began operation in 1960 at the University of Illinois on ILLIAC I when Bitzer was 26, establishing him as the 'father of PLATO'.
early_history_summary: Born January 1, 1934 in East St. Louis and raised in Collinsville, Illinois, Bitzer completed BS (1955), MS (1956), and PhD (1960) degrees in electrical engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. As a young laboratory staffer/faculty path researcher he proposed and directed a working computer-based teaching demonstration that became PLATO I in 1960, launching a multi-decade platform that pioneered touchscreens, online community features, and later motivated his co-invention of the plasma display.
family_context_summary: Born in East St. Louis and grew up in Collinsville, Illinois; contemporaneous obituaries note his father ran a local Plymouth automobile dealership. Detailed wealth or elite-network family status is not strongly documented beyond a small-business household context.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father ran a Plymouth dealership; no clear electrical-engineering or computing domain apprenticeship from parents is documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: University of Illinois CSL, ILLIAC access, PLATO lab, engineering degrees by 26, education-technology mission
evidence_summary: Bitzer's age-26 milestone is multiply sourced: Britannica, University of Illinois materials, and Wikipedia date PLATO's 1960 launch under his direction the same year he finished his Illinois PhD. Subsequent plasma-display invention (1964), national engineering honors, Emmy recognition, and National Inventors Hall of Fame induction confirm long-run impact. Early advantages were primarily institutional—continuous UIUC training and lab access to scarce mainframe facilities—rather than family computing wealth. He later moved to NC State as a distinguished research professor and died in 2024.
starting_point: Born 1934 in East St. Louis and raised in Collinsville, Illinois, in a small-business household (father ran a Plymouth dealership); completed all electrical-engineering degrees at the University of Illinois.
current_position: Died December 10, 2024 at age 90 in Cary, North Carolina; final role: Distinguished University Research Professor of Computer Science (emeritus path) at North Carolina State University; remembered as PLATO's creator and plasma-display co-inventor.

trajectory.event: Directed launch of PLATO I, the first widely recognized computer-based education system, on ILLIAC I at the University of Illinois.
Co-invented the flat plasma display panel to support PLATO terminals, foundational to later flat-panel TV technology.
Received the National Academy of Engineering Vladimir K. Zworykin Award.
Elected to the National Academy of Engineering for leadership applying technology to education.
Shared a Technology & Engineering Emmy Award recognizing plasma display contributions.
Inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame.
Died of congestive heart failure in Cary, North Carolina.
